S1.title: HTTP Error 429 (Too Many Requests) – How to Fix
S1.excerpt:
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests is a client error status code indicating you’ve exceeded the allowed request rate. It’s part of the 4xx family of status codes that signal client-side problems rather than server errors.

Rate limiting acts as traffic control. Just as highways have speed limits, APIs enforce request limits to maintain stability for all users. When you exceed these limits, the server responds with 429 instead of processing your request. [...] The 429 Too Many Requests error code (or HTTP error 429) means you’ve hit the API’s rate limit, where the server temporarily blocks requests to protect itself from overload. This guide shows you how to understand, prevent, and handle 429 errors with practical retry strategies and code examples.

S2.title: 429 Too Many Requests - HTTP | MDN
S2.excerpt:
The HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` client error response status code indicates the client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. This mechanism of asking the client to slow down the rate of requests is commonly called "rate limiting".

A `Retry-After` header may be included to this response to indicate how long a client should wait before making the request again. [...] http

```
GET /reports/mdn HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com 
```

In this example, server-wide rate limiting is active when a client exceeds a set threshold of requests per minute. A 429 response is returned with a `Retry-After` header that indicates requests will be allowed for this client again after 3600 seconds (60 minutes):

http

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests Content-Type: text/html Retry-After: 3600   Too Many Requests

# Too Many Requests

You're doing that too often! Try again later. [...] Implementations of rate limiting vary; restrictions may be server-wide or per resource. S3.excerpt:
# 429 Too Many Requests

Exceeding the allowed request rate triggers the 429 Too Many Requests status code, also known as "rate limiting".

Table of Contents

## Usage

The 429 Too Many Requests status code indicates the number of HTTP requests has exceeded the allowed threshold. This happens, for example, when the server wants to limit the number of API calls in an hour. [...] Queue outgoing requests on the client side. A request queue with a controlled dispatch rate prevents bursts from exceeding the limit. Batch multiple operations into a single API call when the endpoint supports bulk operations.

Cache responses for data not expected to change between requests. Redundant identical calls are the most common source of unnecessary rate-limit consumption. [...] To slow Googlebot down, 429 is the correct status code. 401 and 403 leave the crawl rate unchanged. For Bingbot, a `Crawl-delay` directive in `robots.txt` paces the crawler directly, the alternative Bing documents to status-code throttling.

S4.title: What is HTTP Status 429? | Olostep
S4.excerpt:
HTTP 429 is a client-side requests status code that tells you the client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. HTTP 429 indicates exceeding the API's rate limit - not that something is broken on the server, and not that you are permanently blocked. The status code indicates that access is allowed, but the request rate has exceeded what the server permits within a defined time window. [...] Status line. The response begins with 429 Too Many Requests, a 4xx-class http error confirming it is a client-side issue (request rate), not a server malfunction. The server is not temporarily unable to handle the request - it is actively refusing excessive requests. [...] ## 429 Too Many Requests in Web Scraping and AI Data Pipelines

Large-scale web scraping for e-commerce monitoring, LLM grounding, and agentic research routinely runs into strict rate limits. When your pipeline needs to pull data from thousands of pages across many domains, 429 errors are the primary bottleneck.

bundles.question: For HTTP status code 429 Too Many Requests, which RFC defines this status code (including its name/meaning and status definition)?
bundles.summary:
HTTP status code **429 Too Many Requests** is defined by **RFC 6585 – Additional HTTP Status Codes** [https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc6585.html].

- **Name/meaning:** **429 Too Many Requests** [https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc6585.html].
- **Status definition (RFC 6585, Section 4 “429 Too Many Requests”):** The **429** status code indicates that the **user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time (“rate limiting”)** [https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc6585.html]. The response **SHOULD** include details explaining the condition and **MAY** include a **`Retry-After`** header indicating how long to wait before making a new request [https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc6585.html].

bundles.question: For HTTP status code 429 Too Many Requests, what does this status code mean in HTTP (rate limiting / client request handling semantics)?
bundles.summary:
- **Meaning (HTTP semantics):** `429 Too Many Requests` is a **client error** indicating the client has sent **too many requests in a given amount of time**, and the server is **rate limiting** the client. [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429]
- **Standard requirements (RFC 6585):** The `429` condition corresponds to **rate limiting**; the response **SHOULD** include explanatory details, and **MAY** include a **`Retry-After`** header telling the client **how long to wait before making another request**. [https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6585]
- **Practical usage:** The response is commonly used to tell clients to **slow down and retry later**. The specific limiting policy/counting method is **implementation-defined** (e.g., could be server-wide, per resource, or based on client identity such as IP). [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429]

bundles.question: For HTTP responses with status code 429 Too Many Requests, which response header tells the client how long to wait before retrying (and what is it called)?
bundles.summary: For HTTP **429 Too Many Requests**, the client should use the **`Retry-After`** response header, i.e., it is called the **“Retry-After” header**. MDN states that in a **429** response it **indicates how long to wait before making a new request**. [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Retry-After]
